Issued at 308 PM EDT Wed Oct 28 2026

Rest of Today-Tonight...Florida remains situation between two 
lobes of surface high pressure lingering over the eastern US and a
low pressure system over to just southwest of the Bahamas this 
afternoon. The low has started to elongate as the mid-upper level 
feature begins to lift away from the surface project, allowing the
pressure gradient across our area to loosen a bit and onshore 
flow to relent slightly. Outside of convection and squalls, wind 
gusts have generally peaked around 30 mph this afternoon. However,
winds remains fresh enough that combined with high astronomical 
tides, East Central Florida continues to be subjected to numerous,
dangerous beach and marine hazards, including large rough surf, 
life-threatening rip currents, and during the high tides, coastal 
flooding and beach erosion. Surging moisture in this flow is also 
producing bands of of scattered to numerous showers. Training 
bands of heavy showers could produce a quick 2-3" of rainfall 
leading to minor flooding, and there is a very low chance of 
locally high amounts of +4" producing more impactful flooding. 
Locations already affected by coastal flooding will be especially 
sensitive. There is a Marginal Risk (level 1 of 4) for excessive 
rainfall leading to flash flooding along the Space and Treasure 
Coasts. Bands early this morning already produced 2-4" of rainfall
across a stretch of Martin County. Gusts to 45 mph in these 
bands/marine squalls are possible, and can't completely rule out a
few lightning strikes. Highs are forecast to reach the 80s, but 
wouldn't be surprised if portions of the area fell short due to 
cloud cover and rain, especially the southern counties. Lows 
tonight in the 70s. Still gusty along the coast overnight, but 
gentler winds than previous nights expected for the rest of the 
area.

Thursday-Friday...The northeastern lobe of high pressure is 
forecast to move offshore the New England coast, opening the door 
for the mid-upper level Bahamas low to lift northeast, developing 
a new surface projection in the process. The orphaned surface low 
southwest of the Bahamas is forecast to retrograde west across 
South Florida to the Straits of Florida while weakening into an 
open trough, as the southern high pressure lobe is reinforced and 
builds over the eastern US, bringing the southern flank to 
Florida. The shuffling of these systems will further loosen the 
pressure gradient across Florida some, allowing onshore flow to 
slacken a bit more, though still be breezy and gusty especially in
the afternoons and along the coast. With the peak of this month's
high astronomical tides in the rear view mirror and less windy 
conditions, coastal flooding concerns will gradually diminish, but
minor to locally moderate impacts will continue during the high 
tides (especially the morning high tide) Thursday and likely 
Friday. Beach and marine conditions will also begin to improve, 
but despite the surf looking less threatening, the ocean will 
remain dangerous to bathers as hard to spot life-threatening rip 
currents remain present. Life guards have also reported debris in 
the water. This is the time many surf deaths occur, and beach 
goers are advised to not enter the ocean even as it appears more 
inviting.

Drier air filtering in from the north knocks rain chances down to
20-50% Thursday and 20-40% Friday. Can't completely rule out an 
isolated storm capable of occasional cloud to ground lightning, 
but chances are very low (20% or less). Any storms that manage to 
form and heavy showers will continue to be capable of gusty winds 
to 45 mph. The threat for heavy rainfall leading to flooding also 
diminishes as onshore moving showers become more isolated to 
widely scattered, but areas impacted by coastal flooding will 
remain sensitive to any additional rainfall. Afternoon highs tick 
up a degree or two as cloud cover and rain chances decrease, 
though remain forecast in the L-M80s, on the warmer side for late 
October. Overnight lows also on the warm side in the 70s thanks to
the onshore flow.

Saturday-Tuesday (Modified Previous Discussion)...Surface high
pressure continues to build southward from the Great Lakes this
weekend, strengthening and shifting across the eastern US before
pushing offshore into early next week. Models continues to
indicate development of a mid-level trough over the Deep South and
northeast Gulf, that in turn helps develop an attendant surface
disturbance. However, there remains a fair amount of disagreement
in timing and track of the surface feature by Sunday, especially
from the GFS which develops a closed low off the southeast
seaboard by Monday, while the ECM and CMC remain open troughs
still in the Gulf or over Florida. The official forecast trends
towards the latter two, but confidence for next week is lower than
